claim: Copy-number and point mutations form the basis for most evolutionary novelty through gene duplication and divergence.
source: Together, copy-number and point mutations form the basis for most evolutionary novelty, through the process of gene duplication and divergence.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that represents established scientific understanding in the field.

claim: Selection for increased gene expression often drives the expansion of gene copy-number mutations in microorganisms.
source: In microorganisms, selection for increased gene expression often drives the expansion of gene copy-number mutations, which serves as a crude adaptation, prior to divergence through refining point mutations.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about microbial adaptation mechanisms.

claim: Under high gene expression demand, copy-number and point mutations occur as a combination.
source: In conditions of high gene expression demand, the two mutation types occur as a combination.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental evolution study presented in the manuscript.

claim: Under low gene expression demand, copy-number and point mutations are mutually exclusive.
source: However, under low gene expression demand, copy-number and point mutations are mutually exclusive; here, owing to their higher frequency, adaptation is dominated by copy-number mutations, in a process we term amplification hindrance.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental evolution study presented in the manuscript.

claim: Copy-number mutations may constrain sequence divergence over evolutionary time scales due to high reversal rates and pleiotropic cost.
source: Ultimately, due to high reversal rates and pleiotropic cost, copy-number mutations may not only serve as a crude and transient adaptation, but also constrain sequence divergence over evolutionary time scales.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results and theoretical considerations presented in the manuscript.

claim: Gene duplication occurs orders of magnitude more frequently than point mutations in bacteria, ranging from 10^-6 up to 10^-2 per cell per generation.
source: In bacteria, which are our focus, the duplication of genes or genomic regions occurs orders of magnitude more frequently than point mutations, ranging from 10–6 up to 10–2 per cell per generation (Roth, 1988; Drake et al., 1998; Andersson and Hughes, 2009; Elez et al., 2010; Reams and Roth, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Duplications reverse to single copy or duplicate further at rates between 10^-3 and 10^-1 per cell per generation.
source: At rates between 10–3 and 10–1 per cell per generation duplications will reverse to the single copy (deletion) or duplicate further (amplification) (Roth, 1988; Andersson and Hughes, 2009; Pettersson et al., 2009; Reams and Roth, 2015; Tomanek et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Amplification of a gene or genomic region increases its expression by means of elevated gene dosage.
source: Amplification of a gene or genomic region will, to a first approximation, increase its expression by means of elevated gene dosage (Elde et al., 2012; Gruber et al., 2012; Näsvall et al., 2012; Yona et al., 2015; Steinrueck and Guet, 2017; Belikova et al., 2020; Todd and Selmecki, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Gene amplifications are adaptive in situations requiring rapid increase in gene expression, such as antibiotic resistance, immune evasion, or novel metabolic capabilities.
source: Not surprisingly, due to their high rate of formation, gene amplifications are adaptive in situations where a rapid increase in gene expression is needed: resistance to antibiotics, pesticides or drugs via over-expression of resistance determinants (Prody et al., 1989; Albertson, 2006; Bass and Field, 2011; Nicoloff et al., 2019), immune evasion (Belikova et al., 2020), or novel metabolic capabilities through increased expression of spurious enzymatic side activities (Blount et al., 2020; Richts et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Copy-number mutations differ from point mutations in the nature of their reversibility.
source: This large difference in rates means that a competition between point and copy-number mutations is heavily skewed in favour of the latter (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is inferred from the discussion of mutation rates and reversibility throughout the manuscript.

claim: The experimental system can distinguish between copy-number and point mutations using fluorescent reporters.
source: Importantly, our genetic reporter system allows us to distinguish between the two mutation types. GalK is part of a chromosomal reporter gene cassette and is transcriptionally fused to a yfp gene (Figure 1A). Hence, any increases in galK expression – be it by copy-number or point mutations – can be detected as increases in YFP expression. However, only mutations to the copy-number of the entire galK locus lead to an additional increase in the expression of an independently transcribed cfp gene downstream of galK-yfp (Steinrueck and Guet, 2017; Tomanek et al., 2020; Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and is supported by references to figures and prior publications.

claim: Increases in YFP alone indicate divergence of the galK promoter sequence by point mutations.
source: Hence, increases in yfp alone indicate the divergence of the galK promoter sequence P0 by point mutations, while increases of both fluorophores indicate copy-number mutations of the whole locus.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the experimental design described.

claim: Increases of both YFP and CFP fluorophores indicate copy-number mutations of the whole locus.
source: Hence, increases in yfp alone indicate the divergence of the galK promoter sequence P0 by point mutations, while increases of both fluorophores indicate copy-number mutations of the whole locus.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the experimental design described.

claim: Growth rate increases along with galK expression and saturates at a level dependent on galactose concentration.
source: Growth rate increased along with galK expression and saturated at a certain expression level, which depended on the galactose medium used (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Different galactose concentrations select for different levels of galK expression improvement.
source: Thus, our system allows studying adaptation in environments with different gene expression demands: low concentrations of galactose demand a low level of galK expression (and increasing expression above this level does not add any extra benefit), while high concentrations of galactose demand a higher level of galK expression to obtain maximum growth rate.
evidence: This is inferred from the growth rate data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The IS+ and IS- strains differ solely by the presence of one IS1 element approximately 10 kb downstream of galK.
source: By deleting one copy of IS1, we generated two otherwise isogenic strains of E. coli that differ solely by the presence of one IS1 element approximately 10 kb downstream of galK (Figure 1C), and are thus predicted to show strong differences in their rates of duplication formation at this locus.
evidence: This describes the strain construction performed in the study.

claim: The IS- strain shows a drastic reduction in the ability to undergo galK amplification compared to the IS+ strain.
source: The strain lacking one of the flanking IS1 elements (IS-) showed a drastic reduction in the ability to undergo galK amplification. In contrast to the IS+ strain, very few IS- populations evolved increased CFP expression (Figure 2A – red traces).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental evolution data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In the IS+ strain, the number of amplified populations depends on the galactose environment, with at least twice as many populations amplified in low (0.01%) galactose compared to other environments.
source: Interestingly, in the IS+ strain, the number of populations amplified by the end of the experiment depended on the environment. At least twice as many populations were amplified in the low (0.01%) galactose environment compared to the other two environments (68, 19, and 34 populations for low, intermediate, and high galactose, respectively) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental evolution data.

claim: Maximum CFP fluorescence attained by IS+ populations differed significantly between low (0.01%) and higher (0.1% and 1%) galactose environments.
source: Not only the number of amplified populations, but also the maximum CFP fluorescence attained by IS+ populations differed significantly between the low (0.01%) and higher (0.1% and 1%) galactose environments (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data with statistical testing.

claim: Populations that evolved increases in CFP fluorescence did so within 2 days and maintained this level relatively stably for the duration of the experiment.
source: Populations, which evolved increases in CFP fluorescence, did so within 2 days and maintained this level relatively stably for the duration of the experiment.
evidence: This is observed from the time-course data in the evolution experiments.

claim: The observed difference in the number of galK copies is consistent with the three environments selecting for different levels of increasing gene expression.
source: The observed difference in the number of galK copies is consistent with the observation that the three environments select for different levels of increasing gene expression ('levels of improvement') (Figure 1B) and confirms that amplifications are an efficient way of tuning gene expression (Tomanek et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the expression-growth relationship data with the evolution outcomes.

claim: In the intermediate galactose concentration (0.1%), 5/96 IS- populations exhibit increased YFP fluorescence with ancestral (single-copy) CFP fluorescence.
source: In the intermediate galactose concentration (0.1%) 5/96 IS- populations exhibit increased YFP fluorescence with ancestral (single-copy) CFP fluorescence indicative of promoter mutants, ('YFP+' fraction in Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data.

claim: YFP+ IS- populations evolved in 0.1% galactose carried an amplification extending into galK-yfp but excluding cfp.
source: We hypothesized that the YFP+ populations carried an amplification extending into galK-yfp, yet excluding cfp. Quantitative real-time PCR confirmed our suspicion (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This hypothesis was confirmed by qPCR data.

claim: The IS- strain cannot access the major adaptive route available to the IS+ strain and follows an alternative trajectory through repeat-independent lower-frequency duplication.
source: As the IS- strain cannot undergo the frequent duplication via the two flanking IS elements, it cannot access a major adaptive route available to the IS+ strain. Thus, its adaptation follows an alternative trajectory, which occurs through a repeat-independent lower-frequency duplication with junctions between yfp and cfp (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is inferred from the qPCR and sequencing data showing alternative amplification mechanisms.

claim: IS+ populations from the mixed fraction in intermediate (0.1%) galactose consisted of a single type of mutant with increased YFP/CFP fluorescence relative to ancestral values.
source: Flow cytometry results showed that IS+ populations of the mixed fraction from intermediate (0.1%) galactose (Figure 3A) consisted of a single type of mutant with increased YFP/CFP fluorescence relative to the ancestral values (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is directly observed in the flow cytometry data.

claim: Within IS+ populations from the mixed fraction in 0.1% galactose, only amplified clones harboured an SNP (–30T>A) in P0, not clones with single-copy cfp.
source: To confirm the presence of combination mutants, we randomly picked three populations of the mixed fraction. Sequencing revealed that within these populations, only amplified clones, but not clones with single-copy cfp harboured an SNP (–30T>A) in P0 (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is directly observed from Sanger sequencing data.

claim: IS+ populations from high (1%) galactose mixed fraction harboured cells with combination mutation phenotype and cells with pure amplifications.
source: Similar to intermediate galactose, IS+ populations from the high (1%) galactose mixed fraction (Figure 3B) harboured cells with the combination mutation phenotype and, in addition, cells with pure amplifications (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is directly observed in the flow cytometry data.

claim: Copy-number and point mutations can occur as a combination in environments with sufficiently high gene expression demand.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that copy-number and point mutations can occur as a combination in environments with sufficiently high gene expression demand.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the flow cytometry and sequencing data from intermediate and high galactose environments.

claim: In low (0.01%) galactose, the majority of IS+ populations (68/96) showed increases in CFP fluorescence during the experiment.
source: Surprisingly, and in contrast to the intermediate and high galactose environments, in low galactose adaptive amplification of IS+ populations happened more rapidly with the majority of populations (68/96) showing increases in CFP fluorescence during the course of the experiment (Figure 4A – left top and bottom panel, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data.

claim: Population B1 evolved in 0.01% galactose consisted of ancestral colonies, YFP+ colonies, and a small subpopulation with both increased YFP and CFP (amplified).
source: Consistent with flow cytometry results (Figure 4B), we found colonies with three different fluorescence phenotypes: ancestral, increased YFP ('YFP+'), and a small subpopulation with both, increased YFP and CFP (amplified).
evidence: This is directly observed from colony imaging and flow cytometry.

claim: Sequencing of amplified colonies from population B1 confirmed bona fide amplification without additional promoter SNPs.
source: Sequencing of the amplified colony type confirmed it to be a bona fide amplification without additional promoter SNPs.
evidence: This is directly observed from Sanger sequencing data.

claim: Sequencing of YFP+ colonies from population B1 uncovered two adaptive SNPs in P0 (–30T>A and –37C>T), identical to previously identified promoter mutation 'H5'.
source: Sequencing of the YFP+ colony type uncovered two adaptive SNPs in P0 (–30T>A and –37C>T), which were identical to a previously identified promoter mutation 'H5' (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B; Steinrueck and Guet, 2017; Tomanek et al., 2020).
evidence: This is directly observed from Sanger sequencing data and confirmed by citation to prior work.

claim: All YFP+ IS+ populations evolved in 0.01% galactose harboured either only promoter mutants or a mixed population of a few amplified cells and a majority of promoter mutants.
source: Re-streaking, sequencing and flow cytometry analysis revealed that all populations with elevated YFP and ancestral CFP (Figure 4D – red triangles) harboured either only promoter mutants or a mixed population of a few amplified cells and a majority of promoter mutants (Table 1).
evidence: This is directly observed from sequencing, flow cytometry, and colony analysis data.

claim: No single population with combination mutants was found in the low galactose environment.
source: As opposed to high and intermediate galactose, we did not find a single population with combination mutants in low galactose.
evidence: This is a summary of the comprehensive screening and sequencing results.

claim: Populations with a significant fraction of promoter mutants did not become amplified later in the experiment (with one exception).
source: Quantitative analysis of the fluorescence intensity of patched populations (Figure 4D) confirmed that populations with a significant fraction of promoter mutants (i.e. visibly YFP+ on the agar patch) did not become amplified later in the experiment. As a single exception, population F6 gained the YFP+ phenotype early, but became dominated by gene amplifications by the end of the experiment (Figure 4D – right panel, blue triangle).
evidence: This is directly observed from time-course analysis of colony fluorescence.

claim: All YFP+ populations evolved exclusively from those with ancestral phenotype; no amplified population gained a functional promoter within the time frame of the experiment.
source: Conversely, all YFP+ populations evolved exclusively from those with ancestral phenotype; no single amplified population gained a functional promoter within the time frame of the experiment (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is directly observed from time-course analysis of colony fluorescence.

claim: In low galactose, IS- populations showed a higher fraction of reads carrying adaptive SNPs in P0 than IS+ populations.
source: Intriguingly, in low galactose, we found a higher fraction of reads carrying both adaptive single SNPs (–30T>A and –37C>T) in IS- populations than in the IS+ populations. This is consistent with our hypothesis that the more frequent amplification mutants effectively out-compete point mutations in the low demand environment.
evidence: This is directly observed from amplicon deep sequencing data.

claim: In the low demand environment, a strain which cannot adapt by gene amplification exhibits a higher level of divergence than a strain which frequently adapts by gene amplification.
source: Therefore, we conclude that in the low demand environment a strain which cannot adapt by gene amplification exhibits a higher level of divergence than a strain which frequently adapts by gene amplification.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the amplicon sequencing data comparing IS+ and IS- strains.

claim: After 10 days of evolution in 0.1% galactose, only two out of four random P0 sequences evolved increased galK-yfp expression.
source: After 10 days of evolution, only two out of the four random P0 sequences evolved increased galK-yfp expression (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental evolution data.

claim: P0-1 and P0-3 did not gain any gene duplications or amplifications during evolution.
source: Interestingly, P0-1 and P0-3 did not gain any gene duplications or amplifications.
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental evolution data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The initial expression level conferred by P0-1 and P0-3 might be too low to yield a selective benefit upon gene duplication alone.
source: Given that a plateau exists in the expression growth relation for low levels of expression (Figure 1B), the initial expression level conferred by P0-1 and P0-3 might be too low to yield a selective benefit upon gene duplication alone.
evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from the expression-growth relationship data and the lack of amplification in these strains.

claim: For P0-2, almost every single IS+ population evolved amplifications within the first 2 days of the evolution experiment.
source: For P0-2, the evolutionary dynamics differed from P0. In the IS+ strain, almost every single population evolved amplifications within the first 2 days of the evolution experiment (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental evolution data.

claim: P0-2 exhibits a higher baseline expression level than the other three random promoter sequences.
source: Moreover, it is shifted towards higher values of YFP/CFP relative to values found for P0 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that P0-2 exhibits a higher baseline expression level than all the other three random promoter sequences.
evidence: This is inferred from the YFP/CFP ratio data and growth advantage data.

claim: P0 and P0-2 confer a significant growth advantage over the other two promoters (P0-1 and P0-3).
source: However, in line with the observed evolutionary dynamics, P0 and even more so P0-2 confers a significant growth advantage over the other two promoters (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is directly observed in the growth data.

claim: Six P0-2 IS+ populations that failed to evolve amplifications show an increase in YFP/CFP early in the evolution experiment.
source: Intriguingly, with the majority (88/96) of P0-2 IS+ population amplified, six P0-2 IS+ populations that failed to evolve amplifications show an increase in YFP/CFP early in the evolution experiment (Figure 6B – left panel, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental evolution data.

claim: In the majority of P0-2 clones with increased YFP/CFP (4/6 for IS+, 11/21 for IS-), sequencing revealed mutations in P0-2, including an SNP, a 12 bp deletion, and a 13 bp deletion.
source: Sequencing of randomly picked evolved clones revealed that in the majority (4/6 for IS+, 11/21 for IS-) of clones with increased YFP/CFP indeed harboured a mutation in P0-2, including an SNP, a 12 and a 13 bp deletion (Table 2; Figure 6C).
evidence: This is directly observed from Sanger sequencing data.

claim: Colonies from the same P0-2 populations with ancestral fluorescence harboured ancestral P0-2 sequences, indicating that the observed mutations are causal for increased YFP expression.
source: Importantly, colonies of the same populations but with ancestral fluorescence harboured ancestral P0-2 sequences (Table 1), indicating that the observed mutations (Table 2) are causal for the increased YFP expression.
evidence: This is directly observed from Sanger sequencing data and provides evidence of causality.

claim: Reconstituted P0-2 mutations (12 bp deletion, 13 bp deletion, and SNP) conferred increased YFP expression and increased growth in medium supplemented with galactose.
source: To confirm that the 12 bp deletion mutation, the 13 bp deletion mutation and the SNP were in fact adaptive, we reconstituted these mutations into the ancestral P0-2 strain, where they conferred increased YFP expression (Figure 6D) resulting in increased growth in medium supplemented with galactose (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is directly observed from experimental validation of reconstituted mutants.

claim: P0-2 promoter mutations occurred exclusively in populations with increased YFP but ancestral CFP, and were completely absent in amplified and ancestral colonies.
source: The finding that the promoter mutations were responsible for increased galK-yfp expression was corroborated by the fact that these mutations occurred exclusively in populations with increased YFP but ancestral CFP, and were completely absent in amplified (YFP+CFP+) and ancestral colonies from a random set of 14 IS+ populations (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is directly observed from comprehensive sequencing analysis.

claim: Mutations observed in P0-2 were more diverse than those observed in P0 (seven different mutations including indels, an IS insertion and an SNP in P0-2 versus three different SNPs in P0).
source: It is worth noting that mutations observed in P0-2 were more diverse than those observed in P0 (seven different mutations including indels, an IS insertion and an SNP in P0-2 versus three different SNPs in P0 – compare Tables 1 and 2).
evidence: This is directly observed from comparing sequencing results in Tables 1 and 2.

claim: Amplification can interfere with divergence not only by point mutations but also by small insertions and deletions.
source: Thus, amplification can interfere with divergence not only by point mutations but also by small insertions and deletions.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of diverse mutation types in P0-2.

claim: The majority of IS+ populations with P0-2 become rapidly amplified, with few promoter mutations arising exclusively in the first day in non-amplified populations.
source: Taken together, the facts that (i) the majority of IS+ populations become rapidly amplified, (ii) with few promoter mutations arising exclusively in the first day in non-amplified populations (mutations are mutually exclusive), and (iii) many more promoter mutations occur in IS- populations throughout the evolution experiment strongly suggest that negative epistasis between frequent copy-number mutation and point mutations hinder fixation of the latter.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comprehensive analysis of P0-2 evolution dynamics.

claim: Negative epistasis between frequent copy-number mutations and point mutations hinders fixation of point mutations.
source: Taken together, the facts that (i) the majority of IS+ populations become rapidly amplified, (ii) with few promoter mutations arising exclusively in the first day in non-amplified populations (mutations are mutually exclusive), and (iii) many more promoter mutations occur in IS- populations throughout the evolution experiment strongly suggest that negative epistasis between frequent copy-number mutation and point mutations hinder fixation of the latter.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comprehensive analysis of evolution dynamics across different promoter sequences and environments.

claim: In both low and high demand environments, promoter point mutations evolve at a low rate in a single-copy background.
source: In both environments, promoter point mutations evolve at a low rate in a single-copy background.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental observations across environments.

claim: If rates of copy-number mutation are high, evolutionary dynamics are dominated by amplification.
source: However, if rates of copy-number mutation are high, evolutionary dynamics are dominated by amplification.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing IS+ and IS- strains.

claim: Amplification increases the mutational target size for rarer adaptive point mutations to occur.
source: Irrespective of the environment, this amplification increases the mutational target size for rarer adaptive point mutations to occur.
evidence: This is a theoretical consideration based on the increased number of gene copies.

claim: Only if a strong increase in galK expression is selected for (high demand environment), the beneficial effects of both types of mutation add up, and combination mutations occur.
source: However, only if a strong increase in galK expression is selected for (high demand environment), the beneficial effects of both types of mutation add up, and we observe a combination of amplifications and point mutations to occur, in agreement with the IAD model (Bergthorsson et al., 2007; Näsvall et al., 2012; Andersson et al., 2015; Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and comparison with the IAD model.

claim: In a low demand environment, a single mutational event may be sufficient to provide the necessary gene expression increase.
source: If, however, only a modest level of gene expression increase is selected for (low demand environment) (Figure 1B), a single mutational event may be sufficient to provide it.
evidence: This is inferred from the expression-growth relationship data and the observation of mutually exclusive mutations.

claim: Adaptation is dominated by the more frequent type of mutation (copy-number mutation) in low demand environments.
source: Therefore, adaptation is dominated by the more frequent type of mutation, namely copy-number mutation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations in low galactose.

claim: Amplifications effectively hinder divergence in the low demand environment due to their negative epistatic interaction with point mutations.
source: In other words, amplifications effectively hinder divergence in the low demand environment due to their negative epistatic interaction with point mutations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations and theoretical considerations.

claim: The high rate of amplification results in evolutionary dynamics that slow down divergence via two different non-mutually exclusive mechanisms: clonal interference and negative epistasis.
source: Thus, in a process, which we term amplification hindrance, the high rate of amplification results in evolutionary dynamics that slow down divergence via two different non-mutually exclusive mechanisms: clonal interference and negative epistasis.
evidence: This is a theoretical conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: Clonal interference is an unlikely explanation for the absence of combination mutants in the low galactose environment.
source: However, in our experiments mutation rates can be assumed to be equal across environments. Moreover, in the absence of galK expression (i.e. for the ancestral strain) population sizes are similar across different galactose concentrations (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A). Hence, clonal interference is an unlikely explanation for the absence of combination mutants in the low galactose environment.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental conditions and population size data.

claim: Strains with amplifications evolved in low galactose exhibit both yield and growth rate comparable to that of the promoter mutant strain.
source: In contrast, in the low galactose concentration strains with amplifications evolved in this environment exhibit both yield and growth rate comparable to that of the promoter mutant strain (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This is directly observed in the growth data.

claim: Gaining additional promoter point mutations on top of an amplification would only be beneficial in the higher galactose concentrations, but yield little or no fitness benefit in the low galactose environment.
source: These results suggest that gaining additional promoter point mutations on top of an amplification would only be beneficial in the higher galactose concentrations, but yield little or no fitness benefit in the low galactose environment.
evidence: This is inferred from the growth and yield data comparing amplified and promoter mutant strains.

claim: Under the experimental conditions presented, gene expression demand – and hence negative epistasis – plays a major role in amplification hindrance.
source: Therefore, under the experimental conditions presented here, gene expression demand – and hence negative epistasis – plays a major role in amplification hindrance.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of growth data and epistatic interactions.

claim: The spectrum of adaptive mutations differed drastically between environments selecting for different levels of expression of the same gene.
source: We found that the spectrum of adaptive mutations differed drastically between environments selecting for different levels of expression of the same gene (Figures 1B, 3A and 6A).
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings across different galactose concentrations.

claim: Combination mutants carrying both copy-number and promoter point mutations only evolved under conditions selecting for big increases in the levels of galK expression.
source: Combination mutants carrying both, copy-number and promoter point mutations, only evolved under conditions selecting for big increases in the levels of galK expression.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings from high and intermediate galactose environments.

claim: Selection for only a modest increase in galK expression led to populations adapting by either gene amplifications or point mutations in their random promoter sequence, but not both simultaneously.
source: In contrast, selection for only a modest increase in galK expression lead to populations adapting by either gene amplifications or point mutations in their random promoter sequence, but not both simultaneously.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings from low galactose environment.

claim: If amplification occurred early in the experiment, the random promoter sequence P0 did not diverge within the timespan of the experiment.
source: Moreover, if amplification occurred early in the experiment, the random promoter sequence P0 did not diverge within the timespan of the experiment (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is directly observed from the time-course analysis of populations.

claim: Under a low demand environment, a strain with a high duplication rate (IS+) diverged more slowly compared to a strain with low duplication rate (IS-).
source: Moreover, comparing the number of point mutations between strains that differ solely in the rate of undergoing copy-number mutations in the galK locus, we found that under a low demand environment, a strain with a high duplication rate (IS+) diverged more slowly compared to a strain with low duplication rate (IS-).
evidence: This is directly observed from the amplicon sequencing data comparing IS+ and IS- strains.

claim: Frequent gene amplification hinders the fixation of adaptive point mutations due to most likely negative epistasis between these two different mutation types.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that frequent gene amplification hinders the fixation of adaptive point mutations due to most likely negative epistasis between these two different mutation types.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from all experimental results.

claim: Copy-number mutations are orders of magnitude more frequent than point mutations in bacteria and in eukaryotes.
source: While epistatic interactions can occur with any two adaptive mutations, copy-number mutations are unique, in that they are orders of magnitude more frequent than point mutations in bacteria (Roth, 1988; Drake et al., 1998; Andersson and Hughes, 2009; Elez et al., 2010; Reams and Roth, 2015) and in eukaryotes (Lynch et al., 2008; Lipinski et al., 2011; Schrider et al., 2013; Keith et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The large difference in mutation rates means that competition between point and copy-number mutations is heavily skewed in favour of copy-number mutations.
source: This large difference in rates means that a competition between point and copy-number mutations is heavily skewed in favour of the latter (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a logical inference from the known difference in mutation rates.

claim: Negative epistasis does not slow down adaptation per se, but slows down divergence as populations have reached the fitness peak with an alternative kind of adaptive mutation.
source: Unlike the phenomenon of clonal interference (which occurs between any two beneficial mutations even if their adaptive benefits are additive) (Gerrish and Lenski, 1998), negative epistasis does not slow down adaptation per se, as adaptation is agnostic to whether point or copy-number mutations lead to an improved phenotype. However, negative epistasis slows down divergence as populations have reached the fitness peak with an alternative kind of adaptive mutation.
evidence: This is a theoretical consideration distinguishing negative epistasis from clonal interference.

claim: Negative epistasis between point and copy-number mutations can be expected to occur in any selective condition requiring only a relatively modest increase to a particular biological function.
source: Negative epistasis between point and copy-number mutations can be expected to occur in any selective condition, which requires only a relatively modest increase to a particular biological function, namely an increase in gene expression or enzyme activity by only a few-fold.
evidence: This is a generalization of the findings to broader biological contexts.

claim: Amplification hindrance may be of general relevance for the evolution of gene expression in bacteria and for the evolution of promiscuous enzyme functions.
source: Thus, amplification hindrance may not only be of general relevance for the evolution of gene expression in bacteria, but also for the evolution of promiscuous enzyme functions, which analogous to a barely expressed gene can be enhanced by either copy-number mutations or point mutations in the coding sequence.
evidence: This is a speculation about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: The consensus in the literature has been that copy-number mutations facilitate divergence, either indirectly by providing a first 'crude' adaptation or directly by increasing the target size for point mutations.
source: While we found that amplification slows down divergence under conditions of negative epistasis, the consensus in the literature has been that copy-number mutations not only serve as a first step in the 'relay race of adaptation' (Yona et al., 2015), but that they also facilitate divergence, either indirectly by providing a first 'crude' adaptation to cope with a new environment until more refined adaptation occurs by point mutations, or directly by increasing the target size for point mutations (Andersson and Hughes, 2009; Elde et al., 2012; Yona et al., 2015; Cone et al., 2017; Bayer et al., 2018; Lauer et al., 2018; Todd and Selmecki, 2020).
evidence: This statement summarizes the existing literature consensus and is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Various experimental studies interpreted observations of adaptation to dosage selection in the light of 'amplification as a facilitator of divergence'.
source: Based on it, various experimental studies interpreted observations of adaptation to dosage selection in the light of 'amplification as a facilitator of divergence' (Song et al., 2009; Pränting and Andersson, 2011; Elde et al., 2012; Näsvall et al., 2012; Yona et al., 2012; Yona et al., 2015; Cone et al., 2017; Bayer et al., 2018; Lauer et al., 2018; Todd and Selmecki, 2020).
evidence: This statement summarizes prior experimental work and is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Despite showing that adaptive amplification precedes divergence by point mutations, none of the prior studies provided a direct experimental test of the hypothesis that amplification causes increased rates of divergence.
source: However, despite showing that adaptive amplification precedes divergence by point mutations, none of the studies provided a direct experimental test of the hypothesis that amplification causes increased rates of divergence.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of the prior literature.

claim: Indications for more complex dynamics between amplification and divergence can be found in the existing literature.
source: Intriguingly, indications for more complex dynamics can be found in the existing literature (Yona et al., 2012; Lauer et al., 2018; Richts et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to specific studies.

claim: One study showed that rapid adaptive gene amplification in yeast results in strong clonal interference between lineages.
source: One study showed that rapid adaptive gene amplification in yeast results in strong clonal interference between lineages (Lauer et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: A study in yeast found that adaptation to an abrupt increase in temperature was dominated by rapid copy-number mutation, with SNPs occurring only much later.
source: A second study in yeast found that adaptation to an abrupt increase in temperature was dominated by rapid copy-number mutation, with SNPs occurring only much later (Yona et al., 2012; Yona et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to specific studies.

claim: An experimental evolution study in Bacillus found that adaptation was dominated by copy-number mutations with a surprising lack of promoter mutations.
source: Lastly, an experimental evolution study in Bacillus, adaptation was dominated by copy-number mutations and the authors noted the surprising lack of promoter mutations (Richts et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: The transient dynamics of gene amplification allows tuning of gene expression on short evolutionary time scales in the absence of an evolved promoter.
source: The transient dynamics of gene amplification allows tuning of gene expression on short evolutionary time scales in the absence of an evolved promoter (Tomanek et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: If adaptation by amplification is the fastest and sufficient, other, less frequent, mutations may not have a chance to compete.
source: Our present study proved this intuition wrong, as we uncovered a potentially long-lasting effect resulting from the transient dynamics associated with copy-number mutations: if adaptation by amplification is the fastest and sufficient, other, less frequent, mutations may not have a chance to compete.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Due to pleiotropic cost and high rate of deletion, adaptive amplification returns to the ancestral single-copy state in the absence of selection.
source: Due to the pleiotropic cost often associated with copy-number increases as well as their high rate of deletion, adaptive amplification returns to the ancestral single-copy state in the absence of selection (Andersson and Hughes, 2009; Reams et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Once the selective benefit of the transient adaptation ceased, no change at the level of genomic DNA remains.
source: This means that once the selective benefit of the transient adaptation ceased, no change at the level of genomic DNA remains (Roth, 1996).
evidence: This is a logical consequence of amplification reversal and is supported by a citation.

claim: The idea that gene amplifications act as a transient 'regulatory state' rather than a mutation can be extended by the implication that amplifications could effectively act as buffer against long-lasting point mutations.
source: Therefore, the idea that gene amplifications act as a transient 'regulatory state' rather than a mutation (Roth, 1996; Tomanek et al., 2020) can be extended by an implication found here, namely that amplifications could effectively act as buffer against long-lasting point mutations.
evidence: This is a theoretical extension of prior concepts based on the current findings.

claim: Amplification could repeatedly provide rapid adaptation to selection for increased gene expression, but collapse back to the single-copy ancestral state once selection has subsided and yet hinder sequence divergence each time it does so.
source: In this view, amplification could repeatedly provide rapid adaptation to selection for increased gene expression, but collapse back to the single-copy ancestral state once selection has subsided and yet hinder sequence divergence each time it does so.
evidence: This is a speculation about the long-term evolutionary implications of the findings.

claim: On sufficiently long time scales, the transient dynamics that play out before the fixation of mutations may ultimately shape entire genomes.
source: Thus, on sufficiently long time scales, the transient dynamics that play out before the fixation of mutations may ultimately shape entire genomes (Cvijović et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculation about the long-term evolutionary implications supported by a citation.

claim: Amplification hindrance is in agreement with the observation that gene duplication and divergence is not a dominant force in the expansion of protein families in bacteria.
source: Amplification hindrance is in agreement with the observation that gene duplication and divergence is not a dominant force in the expansion of protein families in bacteria (Treangen and Rocha, 2011; Tria and Martin, 2021).
evidence: This statement connects the findings to prior observations in the literature and is supported by citations.

claim: In all situations where rapid amplification provides sufficient adaptation, amplification hindrance could work as a mutational force that acts to conserve existing genes and their expression level.
source: Consequently, in all situations where rapid amplification provides sufficient adaptation, amplification hindrance could work as a mutational force that – in addition to purifying selection – acts to conserve existing genes and their expression level.
evidence: This is a speculation about the broader evolutionary implications of the findings.

claim: Amplification hindrance prevents beneficial mutations from fixating, unlike purifying selection which affects deleterious alleles only.
source: While purifying selection affects deleterious alleles only, counterintuitively, amplification hindrance prevents beneficial mutations from fixating.
evidence: This is a theoretical distinction highlighting the unique nature of amplification hindrance.

claim: YFP fluorescence is linearly correlated with galK copy-number for clones with ancestral P0 sequence.
source: (B) Colony YFP fluorescence plotted against copy-number relative to a single-copy control strain as determined by qPCR. Linear model fitted to all data points with ancestral P0 sequence. Adjusted R-squared=0.97, p-value = 3.57e-06.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B with statistical analysis.

claim: YFP fluorescence is linearly correlated with CFP fluorescence for clones with ancestral P0 sequence.
source: (C) Colony YFP fluorescence plotted against CFP fluorescence. Linear model fitted to all data points with ancestral P0 sequence. Adjusted R-squared=0.97, p-value = 7.6e-06.
evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C with statistical analysis.

claim: After 12 days of evolution, cells with ancestral YFP and CFP fluorescence were still present in every single amplified population.
source: It is worth noting that after 12 days of evolution, cells with ancestral YFP and CFP fluorescence were still present in every single amplified population.
evidence: This is observed from the flow cytometry data of evolved populations.

claim: Mutants did not spread to complete fixation in any amplified population, highlighting that experiments are capturing transient adaptive dynamics.
source: While some populations consisted of a high fraction of cells with elevated CFP fluorescence, mutants did not yet spread to complete fixation in any of them, highlighting the fact that our experiments are capturing the transient adaptive dynamics.
evidence: This is observed from the flow cytometry data of evolved populations.
